# How to use this file

**Lab 9b starter.** You now execute the analyses you set up in Lab 9a. The data are read in for you; everything else (factor conversions, models, plots, decisions) is yours. Each step has an empty code chunk with hints and an `Your answer` line. Together with your Lab 9a step 1 this is your write-up.

* The data are the **raw files** from the course website: `wworm1.txt`, `wworm2.txt` and `LeprosyScores.txt`.

## Reading the raw data

```{r data-helpers}
# Where the raw data files live on the course website
data_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/refs/heads/main/Data/Labs/"

# Read the first `nrows` lines of a raw text file (the files end with free-text notes that we skip).
# If the file is in your working folder it is used; otherwise it is downloaded from the website.
read_raw <- function(file, nrows) {
  src <- if (file.exists(file)) file else paste0(data_url, file)
  read.table(src, nrows = nrows)
}

# Latin square files: 5 lines (= rows of the field) x 10 numbers = 5 pairs (T, N), one pair per column of the field.
# as.vector() reads a matrix column by column, so row varies fastest, as in the Minitab "stack" commands.
latin_long <- function(raw) {
  m <- as.matrix(raw)
  data.frame(plot   = 1:25,
             trtmnt = as.vector(m[, seq(1, 9, by = 2)]),   # T: treatment code (0 = control, 1-4 = fumigants)
             count  = as.vector(m[, seq(2, 10, by = 2)]),  # N: wireworms per plot
             col    = rep(1:5, each = 5),
             row    = rep(1:5, times = 5))
}

# Leprosy file: 10 patients (lines) x 6 numbers = (before, after) for TRI, TRII and Control side by side.
leprosy_long <- function(raw) {
  m <- as.matrix(raw)
  data.frame(patient   = 1:30,                    # 30 different patients
             treatment = rep(c("TRI", "TRII", "Control"), each = 10),
             before    = c(m[, 1], m[, 3], m[, 5]),
             after     = c(m[, 2], m[, 4], m[, 6]))
}
```

## The recipe (Lab 9b write-up, handout)

| Step | What to do |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | **Construct the model**: list response and explanatory variables; assign symbols, units and scale type; write the statistical model (Lab 9a). |
| 2 | **Execute the model** and plot the residuals against the fitted values. |
| 3 | **Evaluate assumptions**: residuals homogeneous (residual vs fit plot)? normal (histogram, quantile or normal score plot)? If not met, a randomization p-value may be necessary. |
| 4 | **ANOVA**: show source, df, SS; calculate the likelihood ratio (LR) for the full model (all terms). If the evidence is negligible (LR < 20) report LR and the table; otherwise go on to step 7. |
| 7 | **ANOVA**: calculate MS, F and the Type I error (p-values); report the full table. |
| 9 | **Decisions**: first any **interaction** terms (p < alpha: reject H0; p >= alpha: cannot reject). If significant, interpret. If interactions are not significant, decide about the fixed factors and regression terms, then report slopes or means for the significant terms. |

**The three data sets.** All three are **counts**. Counts often have heterogeneous errors (the variance grows with the mean), so you must judge how severe the heterogeneity is, what to do about it, and whether a recomputed p-value by randomization is needed.

Data source: Snedecor and Cochran (1980) *Statistical Methods*, 7th ed., Iowa State University Press.

\newpage

## Data set 1 (wworm1): Latin square

**Step 1 (from Lab 9a).** Model: paste your model here: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### Step 2. Execute the model and plot residuals against fitted values

```{r d1b-model}
# Hints: factor() for trtmnt, row, col; lm(); fitted(); resid().
# Model formula: response ~ explanatory terms (no interactions for a Latin square).
# Transform treatment into a true factor variable: 0 = control   1,2,3,4  = 4 soil fumigants
# w1$trtmnt <- factor(w1$trtmnt, levels = 0:4, labels = c("Control", "Fum1", "Fum2", "Fum3", "Fum4"))
if (!is.factor(w1$trtmnt)) {
  w1$trtmnt <- factor(w1$trtmnt, levels = 0:4,
                      labels = c("Control", "Fum1", "Fum2", "Fum3", "Fum4"))
}
# Set row as factor
w1$row <- factor(w1$row)
# Set column as factor
w1$col <- factor(w1$col)

# Name the model W1mod and write the equation in R with lm() = linear model
W1mod <- lm(count ~ trtmnt + row + col, data = w1)     # Latin square: additive model
# Compute the fitted values \hatYi
W1fit <- fitted(W1mod)
# Compute the residuals e_i
W1res <- resid(W1mod)
```

```{r d1b-resid, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Data set 1: residuals vs fitted (left) and normal scores (right)."}
# Hints: plot(fitted, residuals); abline(h = 0); qqnorm(); qqline()
# Set R graphics layout to a 1-row by 2-column
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) 
# Plot residuals (W1res) against fitted values (W1fit)
# Then add a horizontal dashed reference line (lty = 2) at y = 0 (h = 0)
# representing zero residual error
plot(W1fit, W1res, xlab = "fitted values", ylab = "residuals", main = "Residuals vs fits"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Generate a normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot of the residuals (W1res) 
# assess whether errors follow a normal distribution:
#    qqnorm() : plots sample residual quantiles against theoretical standard normal quantiles
#.   qqline() : overlays a reference line passing through the 1st and 3rd quartiles
#               points should fall close to this line if residuals are normal
qqnorm(W1res, main = "Normal scores")
qqline(W1res)

# Reset the graphics layout back to the default single-panel (1x1) grid so
# subsequent plots are not drawn side by side
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### Step 4. ANOVA: source, df, SS and the likelihood ratio

```{r d1b-lr}
# Hints: anova(model) gives source, df and SS; LR = (1 - r2)^(-n/2) with r2 = summary(model)$r.squared
A1 <- anova(W1mod)
A1
A1[, c("Df", "Sum Sq")]                           # source, df, SS
r2_1 <- summary(W1mod)$r.squared
n_1  <- nrow(w1)
c(r_squared = r2_1, n = n_1, LR = (1 - r2_1)^(-n_1 / 2))   # LR for the full model (all terms)
```

The LR asks the following question: is this model, taken as a whole, any better at explaining the data than a model with no explanatory variables at all?

If LR < 20: the model as a whole barely beats the null model. There is nothing convincing to explain, so there is no point testing individual terms one by one. You report the LR and the ANOVA table (source, df, SS) and stop at step 4.

If LR ≥ 20: the model explains something real, so you move on to step 7 and test which terms (treatment, interaction, covariate) are responsible.

> **Answer.** Report the likelihood ratio and conclude.

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### Is a randomization p-value needed? (step 3 follow-up)

(1) Assumptions are only moderately met
(2) n = 25 is below 30 and p = 0.068 is close to 0.05

Is a randomization p-value needed ?

> **Answer.** : ?

Shuffle the treatment labels and recompute F for treatment (after rows and columns).

```{r d1b-rand}
# This code performs a randomization (permutation) test of the treatment effect (trtmnt) while controlling for row and col effects.
# The treatments were NOT assigned completely at random: in a Latin square every treatment occurs once in every row
# and once in every column. A plain sample(w1$trtmnt) would break this (the same treatment could appear twice in a row
# or column), so the shuffles must keep the Latin-square structure.
# (1) Arrange the observed treatments in a 5 x 5 matrix (rows x columns).
# (2) Permute the rows and the columns of that matrix at random: every result is again a Latin square.
#     (Permuting the treatment labels as well would not change F, because F does not depend on which label names which group.)
# (3) Refit the model with the re-randomized treatments (ts) and extract the F-statistic for treatment.
# (4) The randomization p-value is the proportion of the shuffled F-statistics that are >= the observed F-statistic.

# 1. Arrange the observed treatments into a 5x5 matrix indexed by row and column
T_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = 5, ncol = 5,
                dimnames = list(levels(w1$row), levels(w1$col)))
T_mat[cbind(as.character(w1$row), as.character(w1$col))] <- as.character(w1$trtmnt)

# 2. Compute observed F-statistic and restricted Latin-square null distribution
nrep <- 100
obs_F1 <- anova(lm(count ~ row + col + trtmnt, data = w1))["trtmnt", "F value"]

rand_F1 <- replicate(nrep, {
  # Permute rows and columns independently to preserve the Latin square structure
  T_perm <- T_mat[sample(5), sample(5)]
  # Look the treatments up by POSITION (as.integer): by name (as.character) would undo the shuffle,
  # because the row and column names are permuted together with the cells
  w1$ts  <- factor(T_perm[cbind(as.integer(w1$row), as.integer(w1$col))])
  anova(lm(count ~ row + col + ts, data = w1))["ts", "F value"]
})

c(F_observed = obs_F1, p_randomization = mean(rand_F1 >= obs_F1))
```


F_observed is the F-statistic for the treatment effect from the true data. It measures how much of the variation in counts is explained by differences among the treatment, relative to the unexplained error variation.

p_randomization: It is the proportion of the shuffled F-values that are greater than or equal to F_observed
p_randomization ≈ 0.1 means that about 10% of random Latin-square layouts produce an F as large as 2.90

If the treatments had no effect, about 10% of random Latin-square layouts would produce an F as large as F_observed or larger. That is more than 5%, so we cannot rule out chance as the explanation and we do not reject H0. The evidence is borderline.

> **Answer.** Randomization p $\approx$ 0.08 (F-distribution p = 0.068): a borderline result

```{r d1b-sqrt}
anova(lm(sqrt(count) ~ trtmnt + row + col, data = w1))
```

## Data set 2 (wworm2): two Latin squares (year 1 and year 2)

**Step 1 (from Lab 9a).** Model: paste your model here: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### Step 2. Execute the model

```{r d2b-model}
# Hints: combine the two data frames with rbind() after adding a year column; make year a factor.
# Nested blocks: year:row and year:col; the interaction of interest: year:trtmnt (put terms in this order:
# year, blocks, treatment, interaction).
# w2$trtmnt <- factor(w2$trtmnt, levels = 0:4, labels = c("Control", "Fum1", "Fum2", "Fum3", "Fum4"))
if (!is.factor(w2$trtmnt)) {
  w2$trtmnt <- factor(w2$trtmnt, levels = 0:4,
                      labels = c("Control", "Fum1", "Fum2", "Fum3", "Fum4"))
}
w2$row <- factor(w2$row); w2$col <- factor(w2$col)
both <- rbind(data.frame(w1[, c("trtmnt", "count", "row", "col")], year = "1"),
              data.frame(w2[, c("trtmnt", "count", "row", "col")], year = "2"))
both$year <- factor(both$year)

W2mod <- lm(count ~ year + year:row + year:col + trtmnt + year:trtmnt, data = both)   
# rows, columns nested in year
W2fit <- fitted(W2mod)
W2res <- resid(W2mod)
```

```{r d2b-resid, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Data set 2 (both years): residuals vs fitted (left) and normal scores (right), raw counts."}

qqnorm(W2res, main = "Normal scores"); qqline(W2res)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
cor(W2fit, abs(W2res))
```

### Step 3. Evaluate the assumptions

What was our remedy, dealing with the residuals for data 1 ?

A square-root transformation is the usual remedy for counts. 

```{r d2b-sqrt, fig.width=7, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Data set 2: the same diagnostics on the raw scale (top row) and the square-root scale (bottom row)."}
# Hint: refit the same model with sqrt(count) as the response and compare the residual vs fit plots
W2sq <- lm(sqrt(count) ~ year + year:row + year:col + trtmnt + year:trtmnt, data = both)
W2sqfit <- fitted(W2sq)
W2sqres <- resid(W2sq)

# 2 x 2 layout: top row = raw counts, bottom row = square-root counts
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
# Top row: raw counts
plot(W2fit, W2res, xlab = "fitted values", ylab = "residuals", main = "Raw counts: residuals vs fits"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(W2res, main = "Raw counts: normal scores"); qqline(W2res)
# Bottom row: square-root counts
plot(W2sqfit, W2sqres, xlab = "fitted values", ylab = "residuals", main = "Square root: residuals vs fits"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(W2sqres, main = "Square root: normal scores"); qqline(W2sqres)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Correlation of the fitted values with the absolute residuals (0 = no fan shape): before and after
round(c(raw = cor(W2fit, abs(W2res)), sqrt = cor(W2sqfit, abs(W2sqres))), 2)
```

Randomization (shuffle the treatment labels **within each year**):

```{r d2b-rand}
# Hints: shuffle the treatment labels within each year (ave() with FUN = sample); refit; p = mean(F_random >= F_observed)
# Hints: same idea as data set 1, applied to each year's Latin square separately
# 1. Arrange the observed treatments of each year into a 5x5 matrix indexed by row and column
T1 <- matrix(NA, nrow = 5, ncol = 5, dimnames = list(levels(w1$row), levels(w1$col)))
T1[cbind(as.character(w1$row), as.character(w1$col))] <- as.character(w1$trtmnt)   # year 1 (wworm1)
T2 <- matrix(NA, nrow = 5, ncol = 5, dimnames = list(levels(w2$row), levels(w2$col)))
T2[cbind(as.character(w2$row), as.character(w2$col))] <- as.character(w2$trtmnt)   # year 2 (wworm2)

# 2. Observed F-statistic for treatment and the restricted null distribution
nrep <- 100
obs_F2 <- anova(W2mod)["trtmnt", "F value"]

rand_F2 <- replicate(nrep, {
  # Permute rows and columns independently WITHIN each year (keeps each year a Latin square)
  P1 <- T1[sample(5), sample(5)]
  P2 <- T2[sample(5), sample(5)]
  # 'both' is year 1 followed by year 2, in the same plot order as w1 and w2
  # Look up by POSITION (as.integer), not by name: the names are permuted together with the cells
  both$ts <- factor(c(P1[cbind(as.integer(w1$row), as.integer(w1$col))],
                      P2[cbind(as.integer(w2$row), as.integer(w2$col))]))
  anova(lm(count ~ year + year:row + year:col + ts + year:ts, data = both))["ts", "F value"]
})

c(F_observed = obs_F2, p_randomization = mean(rand_F2 >= obs_F2))
```


> **Answer.** Randomization p $\approx$ 0.003 (re-randomizing each year's Latin square), in agreement with p = 0.003 from the F-distribution: the decision does not depend on the method.

Means for the significant terms (average over years, from the model without the interaction) and interpretation:

```{r d2b-means}
# Hints: tapply(count, trtmnt, mean); standard error = sqrt(MSE / n); summary(model)$coef for contrasts vs the control
W2red <- lm(count ~ year + year:row + year:col + trtmnt, data = both)      # interaction dropped
MSE  <- anova(W2red)["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
tm   <- tapply(both$count, both$trtmnt, mean)
round(rbind(mean = tm, SE = sqrt(MSE / 10)), 2)                              # 10 plots per treatment
round(tapply(both$count, both$year, mean), 2)                                # year means
round(summary(W2red)$coef[grep("trtmnt", rownames(summary(W2red)$coef)), ], 4)   # each fumigant vs control
```

> **Answer.** Mean counts per plot over the two years: Control 10.7, Fum1 9.6, Fum2 14.4, **Fum3 4.8**, Fum4 9.0 (SE about 1.4); year 1 mean 4.9, year 2 mean 14.4. Only **fumigant 3** is clearly lower than the control (about 55 % fewer wireworms); the effect is consistent in both years. Combining the two years turns the borderline year-1 result (p = 0.07) into a clear one (year 2 alone: p = 0.044).

## Data set 3 (leprosy): ANCOVA and alternative models

**Step 1 (from Lab 9a).** Model chosen first: paste your model here: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### Step 2. Execute the model

```{r d3b-model}
# Hints: lm(after ~ before + treatment); first check before ~ treatment and the interaction before * treatment
lp$treatment <- factor(lp$treatment, levels = c("Control", "TRI", "TRII"))

anova(lm(before ~ treatment, data = lp))          # check: baseline score does not depend on treatment

L_slopes <- lm(after ~ before * treatment, data = lp)     # does the slope differ among treatments?
anova(L_slopes)

L3 <- lm(after ~ before + treatment, data = lp)           # M3: ANCOVA with a common slope
L3fit <- fitted(L3); L3res <- resid(L3)
```
Does baseline score depend on treatment?

> **Answer.** Baseline score does not depend on treatment (F = 1.66, p = 0.21).

```{r unified-table}
# Unified table: baseline, raw after-score and baseline-adjusted after-score for each treatment

# 1. The common baseline used for the adjustment: the average baseline score of all 30 patients
before_all <- mean(lp$before)

# 2. One hypothetical patient per treatment, all starting at that common baseline
nd <- data.frame(before = before_all,
                 treatment = factor(c("Control", "TRI", "TRII"), levels = levels(lp$treatment)))

# 3. Adjusted means (and their standard errors) predicted by the ANCOVA model L3
pred <- predict(L3, nd, se.fit = TRUE)

# 4. Put everything side by side in one table
adj_tab <- data.frame(
  Treatment = levels(lp$treatment),
  n         = as.vector(table(lp$treatment)),
  Before    = as.vector(tapply(lp$before, lp$treatment, mean)),   # observed baseline mean
  After_raw = as.vector(tapply(lp$after,  lp$treatment, mean)),   # observed after mean (not adjusted)
  After_adj = pred$fit,                                           # after mean at the common baseline
  SE_adj    = pred$se.fit
)
# Adjustment = how much the baseline correction moved each mean
adj_tab$Adjustment <- adj_tab$After_adj - adj_tab$After_raw
# Difference from the control: before and after adjusting
adj_tab$Diff_raw <- adj_tab$After_raw - adj_tab$After_raw[1]
adj_tab$Diff_adj <- adj_tab$After_adj - adj_tab$After_adj[1]

adj_tab[, -1] <- round(adj_tab[, -1], 2)
adj_tab

# 5. The common baseline and the slope (change in after-score per 1-point increase in baseline)
c(common_baseline = round(before_all, 2), slope = round(unname(coef(L3)["before"]), 2))
```
